text.p: German industry giants Thyssen AG and Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp, a day after Krupp launched a hostile bid for its larger rival, have agreed to talk on setting up a joint steel company, the state government of North Rhine-Westphalia said on Wednesday.

A spokesman for the state government added that the two companies would present a plan to create a jointly-held steel company within eight days and that, if agreed, it would make a takeover of Thyssen by Krupp unnecessary.

"Such a plan of action would make Krupp's offer to Thyssen shareholders irrelevant," a spokesman said, but warned: "Should the talks between the two companies produce no result, then both sides would return to their original positions."

In a rare move in German industry, Krupp on Tuesday launched a hostile takeover bid for Thyssen, offering to pay 435 marks a share, or a premium of some 25 percent on Monday's closing. Shares were suspended from official trade on Tuesday but traded actively on the inofficial grey market.
A merger of the steel activities of both companies would create a steel group equal to European steel giants Usinor Sacilor and British Steel with some 18 million tonnes of annual steel output.
Analysts said the deal would likely be just the first in a wave of restructurings throughout the German and European steel industries, which have been plagued by chronic overcapacity.
